excerpt: Most of the AI papers I liked lately are about how AI fools the people using it. That is more useful to me than another agent with a Sharpe of 3. This is a new Friday list: the week’s research on data, AI and quant trading, with the links. The first one reaches back about three weeks. Crypto and market microstructure Path-Independent Deleveraging Rules (Schlegel and Mamageishvili) Which profitable positions should a perp venue close when liquidations cannot cover a bankrupt account? The authors narrow the fair rules to a one-parameter family. Replayed on Hyperliquid’s ADL of 10 October 2025, intermediate settings “significantly improve on the observed allocation”. Figure 3 in the paper. Right: each rule’s fairness against its risk 24 hours later; lower is better on both. The red square is what Hyperliquid did. Algorithmic Market Making Can Lead to Rough Volatility Through the Order Book (Ramachandran) Market makers updating quotes over different lookback horizons give order flow power-law memory, and rough volatility follows. Six months of Binance data, about 790 million orders, fit the model. Figure 2 in the paper (CC BY-SA 4.0). Left: the Hurst parameter of order activity in BTC, ETH and SOL, spot and perps, per 30-day block. All sit far below the 1/2 of Brownian motion. Settlement Manipulation in Prediction Markets (Dai, Jia and Yu) Traders moved spot to settle Polymarket’s five-minute Bitcoin contract their way, mostly at retail’s expense. It stopped once settlement moved to a 60-second average price. The old FX fixing problem, on a five-minute clock. Figure 12 in the paper. Binance BTC spot through each five-minute cycle. The jump in order flow before the close (grey) flattens under the 60-second average price (orange). AI in the research loop LLM Trading Agents Earn Beta, Not Alpha: A Look-Ahead-Free Benchmark (Wang) In 91 runs of six models, no alpha was significant, and market and style exposure explained a median 78% of the return.
